hints: Look for the link group in the backbone. An amide $\text{CONH}$ or ester $\text{COO}$ link means a small molecule was lost, while a plain carbon chain means no atoms were lost.
For Y, focus on the two carbon backbone. Addition polymers are made from alkenes, so work backwards by restoring the $\text{C=C}$ double bond.
For X and Z, remember each polymer is made from only one type of monomer, so the single monomer must contain both functional groups needed to form the link.
To draw the hydroxy acid and amino acid monomers, split the ester or amide link to give $\text{OH}$ plus $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ or $\text{NH}_2$ plus $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$.
walkthrough:
Spot the link to classify the polymerisation**
Think with me about what holds the chain together. X contains $\text{CO-NH}$ amide links. Z contains $\text{CO-O}$ ester links. Both of those links form with loss of water, so both are condensation polymers. Y has only $\text{C-C}$ single bonds in a long carbon backbone with side chains, with no $\text{C=O}$ or $\text{NH}$ in the backbone. That is the fingerprint of addition polymerisation.

Work backwards for the addition polymer Y**
For addition, picture the reverse of adding across a double bond. The repeat section shows $\text{CH}(\text{COOCH}_3)\text{CH}_2$ repeating. Put the $\text{C=C}$ back between those two carbons. You get $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCO}_2\text{CH}_3$, which is methyl propenoate.

Deduce the single monomer for polyamide X**
X is a polyamide made from one monomer type, so the monomer must be an amino acid with both ends. Cut one $\text{CO-NH}$ bond and add back the atoms of water. The $\text{CO}$ gains $\text{OH}$ and the $\text{NH}$ gains $\text{H}$. Counting the five $\text{CH}_2$ groups between the $\text{N}$ and the $\text{C=O}$ gives $\text{H}_2\text{N}(\text{CH}_2)_5\text{CO}_2\text{H}$, 6-aminohexanoic acid.

Deduce the single monomer for polyester Z**
Do the same splitting for the ester. Z shows $\text{O-CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CO-O}$ repeating. Split the $\text{CO-O}$ link to give $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ on one side and $\text{OH}$ on the other. That gives $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CO}_2\text{H}$, lactic acid or 2-hydroxypropanoic acid. It has both the alcohol and carboxylic acid groups needed for self condensation.

Final answer: X: condensation ; monomer $\text{H}_2\text{N}(\text{CH}_2)_5\text{CO}_2\text{H}$
Y: addition ; monomer $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCO}_2\text{CH}_3$
Z: condensation ; monomer $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CO}_2\text{H}$

hints: Think about what happens to the $\text{NH}_3^+$ and $\text{COO}^-$ charges as pH changes, and what pH makes the positive and negative balance exactly.
walkthrough:
Picture charge balancing at one special pH**
Remember an amino acid can be cationic in strong acid, anionic in strong alkali, and a mix in between. At low pH both the amine and acid are protonated to give an overall $+1$ charge. At high pH both are deprotonated to give an overall $-1$ charge. The isoelectric point is that middle pH where protonation and deprotonation balance so the dominant form is the zwitterion $\text{H}_3\text{N}^+\text{CHRCOO}^-$ with zero net charge.
Final answer: The pH at which the amino acid exists mainly as the zwitterion with net overall charge of zero.

hints: Compare buffer pH 6.0 with each isoelectric point. If pH equals pI the species is neutral, if pH is below pI it is protonated and positive, if pH is above pI it is deprotonated and negative.
Recall that positive ions move toward the negative electrode on the right and negative ions move toward the positive electrode on the left, while neutral zwitterions stay at the start.
walkthrough:
Decide the charge from pH against pI**
Let us line them up together. Buffer pH is 6.0. Glycine has pI 6.0, exactly equal, so it is mainly zwitterionic with zero net charge. Lysine has pI 9.7, buffer pH is well below pI, so the solution is more acidic than its neutral point and the amine groups stay protonated, giving a net positive charge. Glutamic acid has pI 3.2, buffer pH is well above pI, so the solution is more basic than its neutral point and the carboxyl groups are deprotonated, giving a net negative charge.

Translate charge into movement**
Now picture the tank with $+$ on the left and $-$ on the right. Opposites attract. The neutral glycine feels no pull and stays on the cross at the centre where the mixture was applied. The positive lysine is pulled to the $-$ plate on the right. The negative glutamic acid is pulled to the $+$ plate on the left.

Final answer: At pH 6.0: gly (pI 6.0) stays at start centre, neutral.
lys (pI 9.7 > 6.0) positively charged, moves toward negative terminal on right.
glu (pI 3.2 < 6.0) negatively charged, moves toward positive terminal on left.

hints: Compare the new buffer pH 11 with the pI of glycine (6.0) to decide if glycine will be protonated or deprotonated and what sign of charge that gives.
walkthrough:
Apply the same pH against pI logic at pH 11**
Keep the rule in mind. pH 11 is much higher than the pI of glycine, 6.0. That means the environment is strongly basic relative to its neutral point, so glycine loses a proton from the $\text{NH}_3^+$ group to give $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{COO}^-$. With a net negative charge it is now attracted to the positive electrode, so instead of staying at the centre it moves to the left toward the $+$ terminal.
Final answer: Glycine will move toward the positive terminal / to the left, as pH 11 > pI so it is negatively charged.
